claims.claim: Locke grounded private property in the body, treating labor as a world-appropriating activity rooted in the ultimate privacy of the human person.
qualifications: applies specifically to Locke's philosophical justification of appropriation
claims.supporting_excerpt: Locke founded private property on the most privately owned thing there is, “the property [of man] in his own person,” that is, in his own body.

claims.claim: Hedonism and the pursuit of an absent of pain represent the most radical forms of a non-political, totally private way of life centered on bodily sensations.
qualifications: linked to consistent sensualism and the historical tradition of Epicurean and Stoic withdrawal
claims.supporting_excerpt: Hedonism, the doctrine that only bodily sensations are real, is but the most radical form of a non-political, totally private way of life, the true fulfilment of Epicurus’ lathe biōsas kai mē politeuesthai (“live in hiding and do not care about the world”).

definitions.definition: The doctrine that only bodily sensations are real, serving as the most radical form of a non-political, totally private way of life.

distinctions.distinction: Locke's argument for the privacy of appropriation rests on bodily activity, which is distinguished from the very different argument for the privacy of property.

must_not_be_lost: Locke's derivation of private property from the body
The connection between bodily life, labor, and the modern growth of wealth
The characterization of hedonism and bodily pain as the basis for a totally private, non-political life
